design.text: Open-label, uncontrolled retrospective review of clinical courses of patients treated with carglumic acid 100 to 250 mg/kg/day orally

population.text: Patients from birth to adulthood with hyperammonemia due to N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) deficiency; all began treatment during infancy or childhood

citations.quote: The efficacy of Carbaglu for the treatment of hyperammonemia in patients with NAGS deficiency from birth to adulthood was evaluated in a retrospective review of the clinical course of 23 NAGS deficiency patients who all began Carbaglu treatment during infancy or childhood.

endpoint.text: Short-term plasma ammonia level (within 7 days after first carglumic acid treatment); long-term maintenance of normal ammonia assessed as persistence of efficacy

citations.quote: The primary efficacy evaluation was based on carglumatic acid treatment effect on short-term ammonia levels (within 7 days after first carglumatic acid treatment).

indication.text: Carbaglu (carglumic acid) is indicated as adjunctive therapy for the treatment of acute hyperammonemia, and as maintenance therapy for the treatment of chronic hyperammonemia, due to the deficiency of the hepatic enzyme N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS).

target_moa.text: Carglumic acid is a synthetic structural analogue of N-acetylglutamate (NAG), the essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS 1), the first enzyme of the urea cycle; it replaces NAG (the product of NAGS) to activate CPS 1 and allow ammonia to be converted into urea.

citations.quote: Carglumic acid is a synthetic structural analogue of N-acetylglutamate (NAG), which is an essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS 1) in liver mitochondria. CPS 1 is the first enzyme of the urea cycle, which converts ammonia into urea. NAG is the product of N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS), a mitochondrial enzyme. Carglumic acid acts as a replacement for NAG in NAGS

requirement.text: 1604-2. A registry of patients, including infants, with NAGS deficiency being treated with carglumic acid to obtain long-term clinical safety information.

citations.quote: 1604-2. A registry of patients, including infants, with NAGS deficiency being treated with carglumic acid to obtain long-term clinical safety information. Data to be collected will include patient demographics, details of treatment with carglumic acid, other therapies for hyperammonemia, dietary protein management, clinical status, neurocognitive and psychomotor status, growth and development status, and adverse events.

requirement.text: 1604-3. A study of the effects of carglumic acid on pregnancy and fetal outcomes (may be a sub-study within the NAGS deficiency registry).

citations.quote: 1604-3. A study of the effects of carglumic acid on pregnancy and fetal outcomes. This study can be performed as a sub-study within the registry for all patients with NAGS deficiency. Information on pregnancy and fetal outcomes should be submitted annually (in annual reports) and included in the final report submission on the registry at 15 years post-approval.

requirement.text: 1604-4. Complete and submit the final study report for the ongoing in vitro metabolic stability study of N-carbamyl [14C]-glutamic acid in rat, mini-pig, dog, monkey and human hepatocytes.

summary.text: Carbaglu was approved via a Priority NDA for NAGS deficiency, a rare urea cycle disorder, with orphan drug designation (granted January 20, 1998). Efficacy was based on an open-label, uncontrolled retrospective case series of 23 NAGS deficiency patients, and an Endocrinologic and Metabolic Drugs Advisory Committee convened January 13, 2010 voted unanimously (12-0) that the risk/benefit supports approval. Approval carried postmarketing requirements including a 2-year carcinogenicity study and a long-term patient registry.
